Testimony in Opposition to LDs 556 & 667: "An Act to Modernize the Motor Vehicle Inspection Program and Amend the Law Governing Inspection Fees" & "An Act to Modernize the State Motor Vehicle Inspection
Program and the Law Governing Inspection Fees"
Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and the distinguished members of the Committee on Transportation, my name is Harris Van Pate, and I serve as policy analyst for Maine Policy Institute. Maine Policy is a free market think tank, a nonpartisan, non-profit organization that advocates for individual liberty and economic freedom in Maine. Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony in strong opposition to LDs 566 and 667.
LD 566 bill seeks to expand Maine's vehicle inspection regime by authorizing the Chief of the State Police to implement an electronic inspection system and increase the standard inspection fee to $20. Similarly, while LD 667 establishes exceptions to the electronic system and maximum fee requirements, it still falsely supports and expands Maine's unpopular annual vehicle inspection program. While the proposals may be framed as modernization efforts, they do nothing to address the core issue: Maine's vehicle inspection program is unnecessary, ineffective, and burdensome to residents and businesses.
More Technology, More Surveillance, Less Liberty
Mandating electronic inspections opens the door to increased government tracking of private citizens. As digital systems log more data--location, inspection history, vehicle specifics--questions arise about who has access to this information, how it will be stored, and how it might be used. These concerns are not abstract. Government "modernization" efforts frequently expand beyond their original scope, and once surveillance infrastructure is established, it tends to grow, not shrink. Mainers have a right to be wary of efforts that consolidate vehicle and personal data in centralized systems.
Financial Burden Without Clear Benefit
Raising the inspection fee to $20, regardless of the vehicle's age or condition, will burden working Mainers, especially those in rural areas who rely heavily on personal vehicles for basic transportation. And for what purpose? Maine's current inspection program already represents an annual cost to residents, yet it produces no measurable, quantifiable safety benefit. More than 30 states, including many with similarly harsh weather and more vehicle miles traveled, do not require annual inspections. A 2015 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) shows no statistically

significant correlation between vehicle inspection programs and reduced crash rates or fatalities.1
Incentivizing Over-Inspection and Undermining Trust
The clear intent of this bill is to prevent Mainers from "sticker shopping," a practice itself which highlights the futility of vehicle inspection programs. Vehicle inspections are performed by humans and are subject to human error.
Expanding inspection procedures and tying them to digital records may also pressure mechanics and inspectors to err on the side of caution, potentially citing more minor issues or recommending unnecessary repairs out of fear of liability. If an electronic record shows a passed inspection and a vehicle later fails due to an undiagnosed problem, inspectors could be blamed or even held legally responsible. This creates perverse incentives and erodes trust between customers and mechanics.
If injury happens, regardless of fault, the inspectors may be held criminally or civilly liable, if the court feels they were negligent in their inspection. Inspectors may feel paranoid regarding inspections' legal risks, such as a vehicle inspector in Vermont being found guilty of manslaughter,2 or a mechanic in New York paying millions of dollars in a suit over a limousine crash.3 If inspectors are too paranoid about minor wear and tear risks, they may overdiagnose problems and charge drivers more to fix nonexistent or minor issues.
Similarly, if an inspection station disagrees with the assessment of a previous inspection station and undercuts the initial estimate, the State Police, who administer the program, may end up taking action against its inspection license. Whether the electronic inspection system is used to surveil motorists or inspection stations, it's a troubling intrusion on Mainers' privacy.
A Solution in Search of a Problem
LDs 566 and 667 fail to recognize the broader context: the inspection mandate is antiquated. Instead of "modernizing" a broken and outdated program, Maine should follow the lead of the majority of states and move away from mandatory annual inspections altogether. Our focus should be on reforms that reduce costs and restore

Michael Guay Alfred LD 667
Members of the Transportation Committee,
My name is Michael Guay, and I am a proud third-generation shop owner. I operate two licensed inspection stations and one full-service shop in Southern Maine, as well as one inspection station in New Hampshire. I am here today to support bill LD 667. I speak to you as not only a shop owner, but as a parent concerned for the safety of Maines roads.
The importance of vehicle inspections is non-negotiable. I witness the importance of this program daily. On average, my shops conduct approximately 17,000 inspections within a calendar year. The average fail rate is roughly 30% and within that number of failed inspections, 25% of vehicles fail for significant safety reasons. Within your handout, I have provided examples collected over just the last two weeks...as shown these vehicles have rotting subframes, bald tires, and rusted brake lines, among other concerns. These safety failures cannot be addressed if a car is not inspected by a certified technician while on a lift. Please take note that these are the unsafe vehicles that our families are sharing the roads with. This program provides the consumer with the opportunity to perform preventative maintenance on their vehicle, budget for future costly repairs, and prevents substantial operational failure, failure that is inevitable if the customer is not aware of their vehicle's overall health, just like your annual doctor's visit.
This vehicle inspection fee structure update is long overdue, considering the last fee update was over 24 years ago, despite a significant increase in inflation and overhead costs. LD 667 provides auto shop owners with the opportunity to be fairly compensated for the responsibility and liability they assume by providing vehicle inspections. When done properly, a comprehensive inspection takes an average of 25 minutes. Currently, shop labor rates range anywhere from $80-$140 per hour so inspections should cost a minimum of $25-$35. With the current rates that are in place, shops are losing money and valuable time. The proposed pricing scale within LD 667 will allow Maine's inspection stations to remain operational and keep qualified technicians in the field.
I am confident that this electronic system will provide a significant improvement to the overall inspection program. Based on my experience with the electronic program in New Hampshire. This system would help:
-Ensure consistency in inspection practices by providing a template of safety requirements that must be looked at within the inspection process.
- The state will save valuable time and administrative resources by expediting sticker submission, tracking, and updating sticker inventory.
-All issued stickers are logged into the electronic system and readily accessible, should an issue arise, holding inspection stations accountable.
Misinformation has recently circulated about bill LD 667. The purpose of the electronic system is to ensure honesty and accountability amongst technicians who perform the inspections, not for the state to track consumers. Not only does LD 667 streamline the inspection process from an administrative standpoint for the state, but it also maintains the integrity of the inspection program. Therefore, ensuring the safety of all Maine roads and our families who travel them daily. The critical need for vehicle safety inspections cannot be overlooked or undermined.
Thank you for the time. I ask the committee to support LD 667 and this system and fee update.

To the Joint Standing Committee on Transportation April 8th, 2025
Americans for Prosperity Testimony Support of L.D. 667 (H.P. 435) An Act to Modernize the State Motor Vehicle Inspection Program and the Law Governing Inspection Fees.
Honorable Members of the Joint Committee on Transportation,
My name is Rachel Burgin, and I serve as the Deputy Regional State Director for Americans for Prosperity. On behalf of Americans for Prosperity, I write to express our strong opposition to L.D. 667, sponsored by Representative Parry. While this bill is presented as a modernization of Maine's motor vehicle inspection program, it ultimately increases costs, adds regulatory burdens, and continues a system that many other states have already recognized as unnecessary.
L.D. 667 allows the Chief of the State Police to mandate an electronic vehicle inspection program, potentially contracting with private vendors and charging per-inspection fees to already strained local inspection stations. These fees, while capped at the state's cost, represent yet another governmentimposed financial pressure -- one that will inevitably be passed down to Maine's drivers.
Even more concerning is the revised fee structure, which would permit inspection stations to charge up to 2.5 times the state's minimum wage for every inspection. This could push inspection costs well beyond what working families and rural Mainers can reasonably afford. For many, this will feel like yet another regressive tax--one that punishes those who rely most heavily on their vehicles for work, healthcare, and basic daily needs.
The legislation also increases the cost of school bus inspections, again without clear justification or demonstrated benefit. These changes disproportionately affect low-income communities and school districts already facing tight budgets.
It's important to emphasize that more than 30 states across the country do not require routine vehicle inspections for personal vehicles. These states have not seen spikes in accidents or safety issues as a result. Maine's continued insistence on maintaining -- and now expanding -- this inspection regime places our residents at a disadvantage without improving public safety.
Rather than modernizing an outdated and ineffective system, L.D. 667 locks it in, increases its cost, and burdens both consumers and small businesses in the process. Maine should be moving in the direction of reducing unnecessary regulations, not reinforcing them with costly new technologies and arbitrary fee increases.

At Americans for Prosperity, we believe government should empower people, not burden them. L.D. 667 is a step in the wrong direction, and we respectfully urge lawmakers to oppose this legislation in favor of policies that promote freedom, affordability, and real modernization.
We respectfully request that you vote against this bill and support Mainers who are struggling with taxes and fees increased by mandates.
With gratitude,
Rachel Burgin Regional Deputy State Director Americans for Prosperity

Good afternoon, Senator Nangle, Representative Crafts, and fellow members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Transportation:
I am State Representative Wayne R. Parry, and I proudly represent District 140, Arundel, Dayton, and a portion of Lyman. It is an honor to appear before you today for the purpose of introducing L.D. 667, "An Act to Modernize the State Motor Vehicle Inspection Program and the Law Governing Inspection Fees."
For those that were on the Committee during the 131" Legislature, this is almost the exact same bill that was
sponsored by The Honorable Bruce White, who was a member of this panel. The bill passed on a 12-1 vote - ought to pass as amended -- and also passed in the House before failing in the Senate.
Like everything in society today, things need to be modernized. The inspection system is no different. I
understand that many think we should not have an inspection program at all. I am not one of those people. I am like
most people. We get in our cars and drive them. We are not mechanics. If we did not have an inspection program, I would probably get my car fixed when something broke. I look at the inspection sticker as a reminder to get my
car looked at periodically.
I also understand many have had bad experiences at inspection garages -~ either small shops or car dealers. I
have been fortunate over the last 20-25 years to have great small garages to which I have taken my cars. Others are
not so lucky. This is, however, where this electronic system will help. This system will hold garages more
accountable.
Now to the other part of the bill. Is anyone here making the same as they were 25 years ago? The answer is,
"No." Nevertheless, we have a law that says inspection stations can only charge $12.50 for a sticker inspection. This rate has been in effect for roughly 25 years. This subject has come up several times since I have been in the Legislature. Accordingly, as you can see in the bill, I have tied the inspection cost a station can charge to minimum wage. When we, as a Legislature, set the $12.50 fee, the minimum wage was $5.15 -- a difference of nearly 250%. With cost due to inflation and labor, the number should probably be higher. However, even this maybe too much for
some.
This system is not new. New Hampshire has a similar system and also allows market rates for stickers, which I
believe is around $50 currently.
I ask myself, "If we are going to have an inspection program, we need to allow stations to actually recoup at least some of their cost."
In my opinion, the inspection program in Maine makes our roads safer, and like everything else, needs to be
modernized. We need to allow those that do the work to get paid.
Thank you, and I would be happy to answer any questions.

District 140

Arundel, Dayton and Lyman (Part)
